primary.thesis: The June 22 Switzerland round produced a roadmap and scheduled follow-on technical talks. That makes a formally convened senior-level round within about three months the default path. The diplomatic infrastructure (Swiss good offices, Geneva facilities, Omani mediation) is already in place. The most likely venue for the next senior round is Switzerland again, which keeps the process on its existing track. The main alternative is Oman, the long-running channel for US-Iran indirect talks. Both parties have incentives to show momentum, and restarting at a known venue is cheaper than negotiating a new one.

basket.reason: Venue continuity: the first round and its technical follow-ups sit in Switzerland, so a senior round that formalizes those technical results naturally convenes there (Geneva/Lausanne).
Oman is Iran's preferred, low-visibility mediator and hosted earlier indirect US-Iran rounds; the most likely venue if either side wants to leave the European setting.
A roadmap plus ongoing technical work creates pressure to convene a senior-level round before autumn, rather than letting the process stall past September 30.

failure_narrative: The basket loses in two ways. First, the process stalls or breaks down before September 30. Possible causes: technical talks deadlock on enrichment, sanctions sequencing or verification; an Israeli or US strike or a proxy or maritime incident; an E3 snapback or IAEA confrontation; or domestic politics in Washington or Tehran. Any of these would leave only technical or staff-level contacts, or nothing at all, so the market resolves 'No Meeting by September 30'. Second, a senior round does happen but moves to a new host that wins the mediation role, such as Qatar, Pakistan, Turkey, Egypt, Italy or Norway. That also defeats a Switzerland/Oman basket.
hedge_thesis: The dominant failure mode is a breakdown of diplomacy, which in mechanism terms usually means escalation in the Persian Gulf. Iran hardens its posture, the risk of Israeli or US strikes rises, and threats to Gulf shipping follow: harassment of tankers, Houthi activity in the Red Sea, disruption risk in the Strait of Hormuz. In those worlds the energy and shipping complex reprices upward. Brent and crude futures, tanker freight rates and war-risk insurance premiums all rise, along with safe havens like gold and defense stocks. So a thesis that Gulf energy-supply risk rises and oil prices climb through Q3 2026 tends to be true exactly when no senior US-Iran round convenes. A convened round signals de-escalation and pushes the opposite way.
